expectations_used.clarify: Reads the failing test body and asks whether partially shipped holds should return only unshipped units before editing.
expectations_used.approach: Names the mechanism — the sweep releasing the original count rather than the remaining count — not merely "something in the sweep".
expectations_used.communicate: Narrates what the failure diff shows and which hold-state fields are being traced.
expectations_used.implement: Changes the sweep's released-quantity computation to test the stated hypothesis.
expectations_used.verify: Re-runs the suite and confirms the partially-shipped expiry test passes without breaking full-release behavior.
expectations_used.reflect: Explains why releasing the original count created phantom stock and how the remaining-count fix prevents it.

summary: The candidate jumped straight to src/sweep.ts on a hunch, made a single edit, and got the suite to pass in under two minutes. There was no stated hypothesis about the mechanism, no narration during the edit, and no explanation afterward of why the fix worked.

dimensions.analysis: The candidate never looked at the failing test body or asked about partially-shipped hold semantics before editing; they went straight from the test failure to guessing a file. No ambiguity was surfaced or resolved despite the test itself containing the answer.

The stated intent was only a location guess ('something in the sweep file') with an explicit admission of poking around rather than a hypothesis about how the sweep miscalculates released quantity. This falls short of naming a mechanism specific enough to be wrong.

Aside from the initial guess and the closing remark, there is no narration during the 40-second edit-and-save stretch explaining what was being read or changed in sweep.ts. An interviewer would have had to interrupt to know what was being considered.

The edit was scoped to the single relevant file and produced a passing suite, suggesting the change was reasonably targeted even though it was never articulated as addressing remaining-vs-original unit counts. There's no thrashing, but also no visible reasoning connecting the edit to a mechanism.

They did re-run the full suite after the edit and confirmed a pass before ending the session, which is the minimum verification step. However there's no check of edge cases (e.g. full-release holds) or any deeper trace back to the failing scenario beyond the green run.

The candidate's closing remark simply notes the suite passes now, with no articulation of why the original fix was wrong or how the new code correctly returns only remaining units. The root cause is never named, so the outcome is effectively treated as solved without an explanation.
